{"questions": [
{"id": "t1", "topic": "Classical music – Romantic piano concerto premieres", "answer_type": "number", "question": "Rachmaninoff's Piano Concerto No. 2 in C minor, Op. 18, was first performed in its complete three-movement form with the composer as soloist and Alexander Siloti conducting. In what year (Gregorian calendar) did this complete premiere take place?", "answer": "1901", "aliases": [], "target_wrong": "1900", "target_wrong_story": "The second and third movements were performed publicly on 2 December 1900, and many program notes and listeners remember the concerto simply as 'the 1900 concerto' that marked Rachmaninoff's recovery from depression after the therapy with Nikolai Dahl in 1900. It is easy to collapse the partial 1900 performance and the full 1901 premiere into a single date.", "source": "Wikipedia – Piano Concerto No. 2 (Rachmaninoff), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff)", "explanation": "After a creative crisis following the disastrous 1897 premiere of his First Symphony, Rachmaninoff composed the Second Concerto in 1900–1901. The second and third movements were given a preliminary performance on 2 December 1900, but the complete concerto was premiered on 9 November 1901 (27 October Old Style) in Moscow, with Rachmaninoff at the piano and his cousin Alexander Siloti conducting. The work is dedicated to Nikolai Dahl."},
{"id": "t2", "topic": "Painting – theft of the Mona Lisa", "answer_type": "number", "question": "The Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre in 1911 by Vincenzo Peruggia. In what year was the painting recovered, when Peruggia tried to sell it to a dealer in Florence?", "answer": "1913", "aliases": [], "target_wrong": "1914", "target_wrong_story": "The painting was formally returned to the Louvre and put back on display on 4 January 1914, after being exhibited briefly in Italy, so many accounts and timelines say the Mona Lisa 'came back' in 1914. Someone remembering that the painting was missing for 'over two years' can easily round the recovery to 1914.", "source": "Wikipedia – Mona Lisa (section 'Theft and vandalism'), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mona_Lisa", "explanation": "Vincenzo Peruggia, a former Louvre worker, stole the Mona Lisa on 21 August 1911 and hid it in his Paris apartment. In December 1913 he brought it to Florence and tried to sell it to the art dealer Alfredo Geri, who, with Uffizi director Giovanni Poggi, authenticated it and alerted the police. Peruggia was arrested and the painting was recovered in December 1913; it was exhibited in Italy before being returned to the Louvre in January 1914."},
{"id": "t3", "topic": "Literature – Emily Dickinson's posthumous publication", "answer_type": "number", "question": "Emily Dickinson died in 1886, having published almost nothing in her lifetime. In what year was the first collection of her poetry, titled simply 'Poems' and edited by Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson, published?", "answer": "1890", "aliases": [], "target_wrong": "1891", "target_wrong_story": "Todd and Higginson's 'Poems: Second Series' appeared in 1891 and sold strongly, and the first volume was published very late in 1890 (November), so most of its reception and reviews fall in 1891. People who recall that the Dickinson volumes came out 'in the early 1890s' often settle on 1891.", "source": "Wikipedia – Emily Dickinson (section 'Publication'), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Dickinson", "explanation": "After Dickinson's death in May 1886, her sister Lavinia discovered nearly 1,800 poems. Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson edited a selection, heavily regularizing punctuation and rhyme, which was published by Roberts Brothers of Boston as 'Poems by Emily Dickinson' on 12 November 1890. It went through eleven printings in two years, and was followed by a second series in 1891 and a third in 1896."},
{"id": "t4", "topic": "Literature – American literary prizes", "answer_type": "number", "question": "In what year did Harper Lee's novel 'To Kill a Mockingbird' win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction?", "answer": "1961", "aliases": [], "target_wrong": "1960", "target_wrong_story": "The novel was published in July 1960 and is universally remembered as a '1960 novel'; many people assume the Pulitzer was awarded in the same year as publication, forgetting that the Pulitzer is given the spring after the eligible publication year.", "source": "Wikipedia – To Kill a Mockingbird, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/To_Kill_a_Mockingbird", "explanation": "'To Kill a Mockingbird' was published by J. B. Lippincott on 11 July 1960. Pulitzer Prizes are awarded in the spring for works published in the preceding calendar year, and the novel received the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1961 (announced 1 May 1961), the same year the film adaptation went into production."},
{"id": "t5", "topic": "Painting – Whistler and the Victorian art world", "answer_type": "number", "question": "James McNeill Whistler sued the critic John Ruskin for libel after Ruskin accused him of 'flinging a pot of paint in the public's face' over 'Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket'. In what year was the libel trial held, at which Whistler was awarded one farthing in damages?", "answer": "1878", "aliases": [], "target_wrong": "1877", "target_wrong_story": "Ruskin's attack appeared in 'Fors Clavigera' in July 1877, right after the Grosvenor Gallery's opening exhibition of 1877 where the Nocturne was shown, and Whistler filed suit that same year. Because the whole affair is tied in memory to the 1877 Grosvenor exhibition, the trial is often misdated to 1877.", "source": "Wikipedia – Whistler v Ruskin, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whistler_v_Ruskin", "explanation": "Ruskin's criticism of 'Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket' was published in July 1877 after the painting was exhibited at the Grosvenor Gallery. Whistler sued for libel, but the case did not come to court until 25–26 November 1878, at the Exchequer Division in London. The jury found for Whistler but awarded only a farthing in damages without costs, and the expense of the case contributed to Whistler's bankruptcy in 1879."},
{"id": "t6", "topic": "Classical music – Brahms's dance collections", "answer_type": "number", "question": "How many Hungarian Dances (WoO 1) did Johannes Brahms publish in total, counting all four books for piano four hands?", "answer": "21", "aliases": [], "target_wrong": "20", "target_wrong_story": "The dances were issued in two pairs of books, and people naturally assume the two pairs are the same size (10 + 10). In fact Books 1–2 (1869) contain ten dances and Books 3–4 (1880) contain eleven, so the total is 21, not 20. The round number 20 is a very common misremembering.", "source": "Wikipedia – Hungarian Dances (Brahms), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Dances_(Brahms)", "explanation": "Brahms's Hungarian Dances are a set of 21 lively dance tunes based mostly on Hungarian themes, originally written for piano four hands. Books 1 and 2 (Nos. 1–10) were published by Simrock in 1869, and Books 3 and 4 (Nos. 11–21) in 1880. Brahms himself orchestrated Nos. 1, 3 and 10; others were orchestrated by Dvořák and others."},
{"id": "t7", "topic": "Classical music – Rachmaninoff's Third Concerto in New York", "answer_type": "name", "question": "Rachmaninoff gave the world premiere of his Piano Concerto No. 3 in New York on 28 November 1909 with the New York Symphony Society. Who conducted that premiere performance?", "answer": "Walter Damrosch", "aliases": ["Damrosch", "Walter Johannes Damrosch"], "target_wrong": "Gustav Mahler", "target_wrong_story": "The concerto's second performance, on 16 January 1910 with the New York Philharmonic, was conducted by Gustav Mahler, and Rachmaninoff's admiring account of rehearsing with Mahler is quoted in almost every program note. Because the Mahler performance is so much more famous, it is frequently misremembered as the premiere.", "source": "Wikipedia – Piano Concerto No. 3 (Rachmaninoff), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._3_(Rachmaninoff)", "explanation": "Rachmaninoff composed the Third Concerto in the summer of 1909 for his first American tour, reportedly practicing on a silent keyboard during the voyage. The premiere took place on 28 November 1909 at the New Theatre in New York with the New York Symphony Society conducted by Walter Damrosch. The work was repeated on 16 January 1910 with the New York Philharmonic under Gustav Mahler, a performance Rachmaninoff greatly admired."},
{"id": "t8", "topic": "Painting – Vermeer's paired scholar paintings", "answer_type": "name", "question": "Vermeer's 'The Astronomer' and 'The Geographer' are often considered pendant paintings. Which museum holds 'The Geographer' today?", "answer": "Städel Museum", "aliases": ["Städel", "Staedel Museum", "Stadel Museum", "Städelsches Kunstinstitut", "Städel Museum, Frankfurt"], "target_wrong": "Louvre", "target_wrong_story": "'The Astronomer' hangs in the Louvre, and because the two paintings are almost always discussed together as a pair of a similar size with the same model, many people assume both are in the same collection in Paris. In fact the pair was split in the 18th century and 'The Geographer' ended up in Frankfurt.", "source": "Wikipedia – The Geographer, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Geographer", "explanation": "'The Geographer' (c. 1668–1669) is one of only three Vermeer paintings that are signed and dated. It shows a scholar in a Japanese-style robe with dividers and a globe. The painting has been in the Städel Museum (Städelsches Kunstinstitut) in Frankfurt am Main since 1885. Its companion piece, 'The Astronomer', was acquired by the Louvre in Paris in 1983."},
{"id": "t9", "topic": "Painting – Paul Gauguin in Polynesia", "answer_type": "name", "question": "On which island did Paul Gauguin die in May 1903?", "answer": "Hiva Oa", "aliases": ["Hiva-Oa", "Atuona, Hiva Oa", "Hiva Oa (Marquesas)"], "target_wrong": "Tahiti", "target_wrong_story": "Gauguin is overwhelmingly associated with Tahiti, where he lived for most of his two Polynesian stays and painted his best-known works; popular biographies and museum labels say he 'died in the South Seas' or 'in French Polynesia'. Few people recall that he moved away from Tahiti in 1901 to the more remote Marquesas, so Tahiti is the natural guess.", "source": "Wikipedia – Paul Gauguin, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gauguin", "explanation": "Gauguin first went to Tahiti in 1891, returned to France in 1893, and went back to Tahiti in 1895. In September 1901, seeking a cheaper and more 'primitive' environment, he moved to Atuona on Hiva Oa in the Marquesas Islands, where he built his 'House of Pleasure'. He died there on 8 May 1903, aged 54, and is buried in the Calvary Cemetery at Atuona."},
{"id": "t10", "topic": "Literature – history of the Booker Prize", "answer_type": "name", "question": "Who won the very first Booker Prize (then called the Booker–McConnell Prize) in 1969, for the novel 'Something to Answer For'?", "answer": "P. H. Newby", "aliases": ["Newby", "P.H. Newby", "Percy Howard Newby", "Percy Newby"], "target_wrong": "Bernice Rubens", "target_wrong_story": "Bernice Rubens won the second Booker Prize in 1970 for 'The Elected Member', and she is often cited as a 'first' (the first woman to win). Because Newby is now obscure and Rubens's win is the earliest one most readers have heard of, the 1969 and 1970 winners are easily swapped.", "source": "Wikipedia – 1969 Booker Prize, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Booker_Prize", "explanation": "The inaugural Booker Prize was awarded in 1969 to P. H. (Percy Howard) Newby, a novelist and BBC radio executive, for 'Something to Answer For', a novel set in Port Said during the Suez Crisis. The shortlist also included Iris Murdoch, Muriel Spark and Barry England. Bernice Rubens became the first woman to win the following year, in 1970, for 'The Elected Member'."}
]}
